title: Herbs & Smell Garden
strapline: Crush a leaf, take a sniff — what does it remind you of?
intent: Smell is a powerful, under-used sense, and a herb garden gives children rich, real, memorable things to notice with their noses.
Crushing, tearing, rubbing and pounding herbs is satisfying fine-motor work with an instant fragrant reward.
Growing and tending real herbs connects children to living things, seasons and where food and flavour come from.
Scents unlock unusually rich, personal talk — this smells like Grandma's kitchen, like toothpaste, like dinner.
It's a calming, sensory, inclusive activity that even very young or reluctant children can share in.
implementation: Grow or gather strongly-scented herbs — mint, rosemary, lavender, basil, lemon balm — where children can pick and crush them.
Provide mortars and pestles, small bowls and water to pound, mix and make 'potions' and 'perfumes'.
Sit alongside and model noticing: 'Ooh, smell this one — it's so sharp. What does it remind you of?'
Encourage description and comparison — which is strongest, sweetest, most surprising.
Feed in the names and a little knowledge — this is mint, we put it in cooking, it grows back every year.
Extend into potion-making, scented playdough, or drying herbs to keep.
Involve families' food and cooking so the herbs connect to real, home experiences.
key_questions: What does this herb smell like — does it remind you of anything?
Which one is the strongest? Which do you like best?
What happens to the smell when you crush or rub the leaf?
Where do you think we might use this herb — what's it for?
How could we describe this smell to a friend who can't smell it?

impact.text: Children explore the herbs with their senses, especially smell, and notice and compare the different scents.
Children crush, tear, pound and mix with growing hand strength and control.
Children find rich, personal words to describe smells and what they remind them of.
Children tend and talk about the growing herbs, connecting them to food, cooking and living things.
Children invent potions and perfumes, combining herbs and water with their own purpose.
Children share the smelling and mixing calmly alongside others, taking turns with the tools.

enhancements: Pots of strongly-scented growing herbs children may pick from.
Mortars and pestles, bowls, spoons and water for potions and perfumes.
Scent pots or bags (herbs, spices, citrus peel) for a smelling-and-guessing game.
Scented playdough made with the herbs.
A drying line or rack to preserve herbs and notice how they change.
Links to cooking — adding herbs to real food the children help prepare.

playing_exploring: Children explore with a sense they rarely get to lead with, noticing scents deeply.
They test what crushing, mixing and adding water does to the smell.
active_learning: Children become absorbed in making and refining their potions and perfumes.
creating_thinking: Children combine herbs with intent, compare the results and invent their own recipes.
